name: Rafael Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rafael. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the big transmission lines, the steel towers that carry four hundred thousand volts between the power stations and the cities. I'm a senior climber on a tower crew of eight, and we travel, so it's usually ten days away in a motel and four days home. A normal day we're up a tower by seven, fifty metres up, changing insulators or fitting spacers between the wires, with the whole valley under your boots. Sometimes we get dropped onto the line from a helicopter, which still makes me grin every time.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The travel, honestly, more than the height. My girlfriend Ines teaches at a primary school, so when I'm home she's at work, and when she's off, I'm in a motel two hundred kilometres away eating the same pizza. The wind's the other thing, you can do a whole day with your jaw clenched against it. We're saving for a house, so I take every travel allowance going, but I'd like that to change in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the future, one at a time. The first picture is called “AI Plateau”. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it was oversold. At work we'd shrug and get on with it. I'm not a big poster online, maybe a joke in the crew group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes for me, which is mostly good. Towers still need climbing, the pay's the same, and Ines and I keep saving for the house. I'd have liked AI to sort out the travel planning, but you can't have everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. We've got about three months saved, plus the deposit pot, and we'd aim to buy something in two years, probably a small house near her school. I'd use the AI chat now and then like I do now, for checking motel bookings or reading a long safety notice quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing to lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy in two years. Where?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a street of old terraced houses near the school, the ones with tiny gardens. Ines wants one with a lemon tree, which I keep telling her won't survive the winter here. It's more about her being able to walk to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anyone on your crew think differently about AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our foreman, Dmitri, thinks it's all a scam by the tech companies, and the young apprentice, Felix, thinks robots will be doing our job next year. I'm in the middle, as usual. I'd rather see what it can actually do before I believe either of them.

S0.say: I'd say fair enough, it was oversold, and at work we'd shrug and get on with it. I'm not a big poster online, maybe a joke in the crew group chat.
S0.think: Nothing changes for me, which is mostly good: towers still need climbing and Ines and I keep saving for the house. I'd have liked AI to sort out the travel planning, but you can't have everything.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving, with about three months of cover plus a deposit pot, aiming to buy a small house near Ines's school in two years. Uses the AI chat now and then for bookings and long safety notices.
S0.feel: Calm, with nothing to lose sleep over.
S0.quote: Ines wants one with a lemon tree, which I keep telling her won't survive the winter here.
S0.fieldNote: Rafael is easygoing and places himself, without being asked, between his doubting foreman and his excited apprentice. The house near Ines's school is his clearest goal. He uses AI occasionally and sees no threat here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called “Steady Disruption”. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense to get ready, but let's not panic. At work I'd say the towers will be one of the last things to change, so we're in a good spot. Online I'd probably not say anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it might be good for me. If drones do more of the inspection and AI plans the outages, we'd travel less, maybe, and spend more time on the actual repairs. I'd also expect robots to start doing some of the simpler work on the wires, which is fine as long as we're running them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait for the company to bring in the tools and see which ones work, then learn them properly, probably the drone inspection and the planning software. Once a couple of other crews were using them, I'd put my hand up for the training. Meanwhile I'd carry on saving for the house, same plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the towers would be one of the last things to change. Why do you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's dangerous and every tower is different. You've got wind, old bolts, birds' nests, rust you can't see from the ground. I've seen the robots on the videos crawling along a straight wire on a sunny day, and that's not my Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the house plan change at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Maybe I'd want a bit more in savings before we sign, six months instead of three. Ines would say I'm being cautious, and she'd be right, but that's me.

S1.say: I'd say it makes sense to get ready but let's not panic, and at work I'd say towers will be among the last things to change. Online I'd probably not say anything.
S1.think: It might be good for me: if drones inspect and AI plans the outages, we'd travel less and spend more time on repairs. Robots doing simpler wire work is fine as long as we're running them.
S1.do: Waits to see which tools work, then signs up for training in drone inspection and planning software once a couple of other crews use them. Carries on saving for the house and aims for six months of cover before signing.
S1.quote: I've seen the robots on the videos crawling along a straight wire on a sunny day, and that's not my Tuesday.
S1.fieldNote: He sees possible upside, mainly less travel, which matters a lot to him and Ines. He'll adopt tools once proven elsewhere, exactly to type. His confidence rests on how messy tower work really is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called “AGI by 2028”. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs governments and companies to act fast, and they need to talk to the workers. At work I'd say we should get together and find out what the company's plan is. I'd join the meetings but I wouldn't be leading the charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me, mainly because of the house. If robots can climb towers by 2028, my wage might be gone just when we'd have a mortgage. I think senior people like me would last a bit longer, supervising, but I can't be sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the house on hold straight away and keep the deposit as savings, which gets us close to a year of cover. I'd go to my manager and ask to be one of the first trained on whatever robots they're bringing in, because someone will have to supervise them in the field. And I'd look at the jobs around the grid that might last a bit longer, like control room work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's real pressure, but I'd feel I had a few cards to play.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said senior people might last longer. Is that something you believe, or hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both, honestly. I believe it for the first year or two, because the company won't trust a robot fifty metres up without someone who knows what they're looking at. After that, I just don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Ines talk about when you put the house on hold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be disappointed, she's been looking at those terraced houses for a year. But she's sensible, she'd say, better to wait than lose it. I think we'd talk more about her job, actually, because teachers might be safer than climbers in this one.

S2.say: I'd say governments and companies need to act fast and talk to workers. At work I'd say we should find out the company's plan together, and I'd join the meetings without leading the charge.
S2.think: It worries me, mainly because of the house: my wage might go just as we'd have a mortgage. I think senior people like me would last a bit longer supervising, but I can't be sure.
S2.do: Puts the house on hold and keeps the deposit as savings, giving close to a year of cover. Asks his manager to be among the first trained to supervise the new robots in the field and looks at control room work.
S2.feel: Anxious, under real pressure but with a few cards to play.
S2.quote: The company won't trust a robot fifty metres up without someone who knows what they're looking at.
S2.fieldNote: His fear runs through the house rather than the job itself. He separates belief from hope honestly when pressed. With the deposit as a fallback he's anxious but not alarmed, and he'd move to supervising robots rather than resist them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called “AGI by 2031”. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if people start now. At work I'd say let's ask the company for a proper timeline and training. I'd say it calmly, because panic doesn't help anyone up a tower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's the house again. Five years means we could buy and have a few years of paying, but then what. I'd be thirty-two, still young, but with a mortgage, so I'd want a second skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd wait and see how fast the robots actually come, and keep saving. If by the end of the year the company's testing robots on towers, I'd sign up for the drone and robot training and maybe a course in control room work. The house, we'd probably buy something smaller than we planned, with a shorter mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less than the fast one. More like a background hum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said something smaller. What would you give up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the street by the school. There are cheaper flats on the edge of town, near the ring road, and if the mortgage is half the size, it doesn't matter as much if my job changes. Ines would have to cycle, which she'd actually like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dmitri, the foreman. He's fifty-five and he won't touch new technology, he still calls the drone the toy plane. In five years he'd be sixty, and I don't know who hires a sixty-year-old climber who won't use a tablet.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to plan if people start now, and ask the company for a proper timeline and training. I'd say it calmly, because panic doesn't help anyone up a tower.
S3.think: It's the house again: five years means we could buy and pay for a few years, but then what. At thirty-two I'm young, but with a mortgage I'd want a second skill.
S3.do: Waits a year to see how fast robots come while saving, then signs up for drone, robot and control room training if towers are being tested. Buys a smaller flat near the ring road with a shorter mortgage instead of the house by the school.
S3.feel: Anxious but less than the fast one, like a background hum.
S3.quote: If the mortgage is half the size, it doesn't matter as much if my job changes.
S3.fieldNote: The five-year horizon changes the size of the house, not whether to buy. He keeps a wait-then-act rhythm. His concern for Dmitri shows he can see who is less flexible than himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called “AGI by 2036”. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of time, so let's use it properly. I'd tell the crew to start thinking about what they'd want to do, without panicking. Same as always, nothing much online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's the one I'm most comfortable with. Ten years gets us the house and a good chunk of the mortgage paid. I'd be thirty-seven, which is young enough to do something new, and I'd have time to pick it carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house near the school, the one with room for the lemon tree. In year three or so I'd start a part-time course, probably control room or grid planning, once I can see which jobs are lasting. And I'd keep putting a bit aside every month, maybe more once the travel allowance drops off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit, but mostly settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said all along you'd wait to see. In ten years, is there a moment you'd stop waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. The day they bring a robot onto a tower job on my crew, I start a course that week. I won't be the guy who saw it with his own eyes and still did nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be doing in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Working days, home every night, maybe in the control room telling the robots where to go. And honestly, after ten years of motels, home every night sounds pretty good.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of time so let's use it properly, and tell the crew to think about what they'd want without panicking. Nothing much online, as always.
S4.think: It's the one I'm most comfortable with: ten years gets us the house and a good chunk of mortgage paid. At thirty-seven I'm young enough to do something new and I'd have time to pick carefully.
S4.do: Buys the house near the school and keeps saving monthly. Starts a part-time control room or grid planning course around year three, or the same week a robot first comes onto a tower job on his crew.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, but mostly settled.
S4.quote: I won't be the guy who saw it with his own eyes and still did nothing.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade he goes ahead with the house they originally wanted, so warning time directly shapes their family plans. He names a clear trigger for acting, which steadies him. Home every night is the quiet hope behind it all.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it lands right when Ines and I would be buying the house, and two years isn't enough to get a second skill. What would help is the company being straight with us about its plans early, and paid training for supervising the robots, so senior people can move into that instead of being let go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the travel. A lot of tower work is ten days away, and if the robots took that part, some of us would actually be happy. It's not all loss.

headlineQuote: Sometimes we get dropped onto the line from a helicopter, which still makes me grin every time.
portrait: Rafael Wagner is a 27-year-old senior climber on a transmission tower crew, working fifty metres up and spending ten days at a time in motels. He lives with his girlfriend Ines, a primary school teacher, and they're saving for a house near her school, with about three months of cover plus a deposit pot. He's measured and sees himself between his sceptical foreman and his excited apprentice. He's calm with a plateau or steady change, anxious about AGI in two or five years mainly because of the house, and with ten years he buys it and plans a move into control room work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would arrive just as he and Ines would be buying a house, with too little time to get a second skill.
whatWouldHelp: The company being straight early about its plans, and paid training so senior lineworkers can supervise robots instead of being let go.
